title: Baby sea turtles make history in California
lead: For the first time, baby sea turtles from nests on the US West Coast have gone into the Pacific Ocean.
body: In September 2026, people found something surprising on 2 beaches in Southern California: sea turtle nests! Scientists say it was the first time that sea turtles laid eggs naturally on the West Coast of the USA. The mums were olive ridleys, one of the smallest kinds of sea turtle.

But the beaches were not safe because big storms were coming. So, on 25 September, experts moved about 200 eggs to the Aquarium of the Pacific, in Long Beach. They put the eggs in sand, in a special warm room, and they waited for about 2 months.
Some of the eggs hatched, and the aquarium has released more than 50 hatchlings into the ocean. It happened at night on 14 and 15 November, at Seal Beach and Huntington Beach.
Life is hard for baby sea turtles: only about 1 in 1,000 becomes an adult. Scientists think that warmer ocean water may be one reason why the turtles came so far north.

title: Young inventors win prizes for their games
lead: In the USA, a competition gives prizes to children and teenagers who invent new toys and games.
body: Do you like board games? Do you have ideas for new ones? In the USA, young people can enter a competition called the Young Inventor Challenge. On 7 November 2026, the winners got their awards at the Chicago Toy & Game Fair, in Illinois.

This year, there were nearly 250 inventions from 7 countries, for example the USA, Canada, Spain and South Korea. The inventors were aged 6 to 18. Experts from the toy industry worked for almost 300 hours to choose the best games.

Julia Black, from Massachusetts, is in 8th grade, like a pupil in 4e in France. Her game won the prize for the most innovative idea. It is a matching game with bird calls, the songs of birds. And it is for everybody: blind and sighted players can play together!
Younger children won prizes too. William Safianoff, a 5th grader from Connecticut, invented a game about monarch butterflies, and Vidal Opanuga, from Canada, won a prize for his game, Elementiq.

title: Voyager 1: one light-day from Earth!
lead: On 18 November 2026, a NASA spacecraft was so far away that light needed 24 hours to reach it.
body: Voyager 1 is a small spacecraft. NASA launched it on 5 September 1977, so it is 49 years old! It visited Jupiter and Saturn. Then it continued its trip, and in 2012 it went into interstellar space, the space between the stars.

On 18 November 2026, Voyager 1 was one light-day from Earth. Light needs 24 hours to go from Earth to the spacecraft. It is about 25.9 billion kilometres away! No other object made by humans is so far.
Scientists talk to Voyager with very big antennas. A message takes 1 day to arrive, and the answer takes 1 more day. The spacecraft travels at about 61,000 kilometres per hour.
Voyager 1 also carries a golden record with sounds and pictures from Earth. It is a message for aliens, maybe!

title: 12 'lost' corals are back on the Great Barrier Reef
lead: Scientists in Australia have used DNA to show that 12 forgotten corals are real, separate species.
body: Corals look like plants or rocks, but they are animals! The Great Barrier Reef, in Australia, is the biggest coral reef in the world. In November 2026, scientists from James Cook University and the Queensland Museum announced good news: 12 'lost' coral species are back!

Some of these corals have been known to science for more than 100 years. But experts thought they were just other species with a different shape, because they looked very similar. So the 12 species disappeared from the lists.

To find the truth, the team needed DNA. But old coral skeletons in museums have no DNA. So the scientists went back to the places where each coral was first found and collected living corals. Their DNA showed that the 12 corals are different species.
Why is it important? A coral that looks common can really be several species, and each one lives in a smaller area. So some corals may be in more danger than we thought.
